extraction_method: manual structured extraction from Vallas & Schor 2020, 'What Do Platforms Do? Understanding the Gig Economy', Annual Review of Sociology 46:273-294

worker_heterogeneity_trope_rejection.value: Most gig / crowdwork workers are NOT the 'precarious, dependent, full-time' stereotype. The accumulation of survey and qualitative evidence shows substantial diversity across education, earnings, reliance-on-platform, and demographic profile.
worker_heterogeneity_trope_rejection.quote: An accumulation of survey and qualitative evidence on the diversity of platform workers typically finds that the trope of the precarious, dependent, full-time worker is not easily squared with the situations of most workers performing gig and crowdwork (Forde et al. 2017)

value: Architects/technologists: founders, highly skilled employees, independent contractors
Professional freelancers: designers, writers, cloud-based consultants, content producers, influencers — variable earnings, often entrepreneurial identity
On-demand service workers: ride-hail drivers (Uber, Lyft), delivery workers (DoorDash, Instacart), TaskRabbit
Microtaskers: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT), Figure Eight — priced under extreme global competition, cannot earn a living wage in wealthy countries

racial_bias_in_ratings.value: Workers of color — especially women of color — receive fewer reviews and lower ratings on platforms like TaskRabbit and Fiverr (Hannák et al. 2017)
racial_bias_in_ratings.quote: women and, particularly, workers of color receive fewer reviews and lower ratings

earnings_volatility_source.value: Platform workers bear all the costs of inadequate demand and lost earnings — no employer-side compensation for low-demand periods
earnings_volatility_source.quote: Platform workers bear all the costs of inadequate demand and lost earnings

microtasker_living_wage_impossibility.value: Microtasking priced under extremely competitive global-north/south conditions; earning a living wage in wealthy countries through microtasking is limited
microtasker_living_wage_impossibility.quote: the ability to earn a living wage in wealthy countries through microtasking is limited

supplemental_vs_primary_income.value: Many owners of cars, homes, tools, and other goods monetize latent value of these assets, reducing dependence on labor income — platform work often as supplement not primary income

worker_classification.value: Platforms almost always classify workers as independent contractors — especially problematic in the United States where social insurance (unemployment, health, retirement) is directly tied to employment status
worker_classification.quote: While platforms almost always classify workers as independent contractors, this feature was most problematic in the United States, where social insurance is directly tied to employment status

algorithmic_opacity.value: Algorithms render the labor process legible to employers but opaque to employees — workers cannot see how tasks, prices, and ratings are determined
algorithmic_opacity.quote: The effect is to render the labor process more legible to employers than employees (Calo & Rosenblat 2017)

algorithmic_volatility.value: Platform work varies over time due to frequent changes in algorithmic designs, market conditions, and regulatory policy — workers cannot stabilize their expectations
algorithmic_volatility.quote: Platform work also varies over time, owing to frequent changes in algorithmic designs, market conditions, and regulatory policy

deactivation_risk.value: Platforms retain unilateral power to deactivate worker accounts, often via opaque algorithmic or customer-rating triggers. Deactivation terminates the worker's income overnight.
deactivation_risk.source_ref: implied throughout; direct at p13 tip-stealing / worker-organizing context

worker_of_color_rating_gap.value: See demographics/racial_bias_in_ratings — creates compounding income effect where lower-rated workers get fewer jobs

tip_stealing_historical_case.value: Instacart tip-stealing media campaign (early 2019) led to policy change after public pressure. Illustrates platform-as-intermediary fraud vector where worker-visible tips are diverted into base-pay offsets.
tip_stealing_historical_case.quote: In early 2019, a media campaign against tip stealing by Instacart was successful

account_access_as_livelihood_gateway.value: Platform account = livelihood. Any account compromise (ATO, credential stuffing, SIM swap) immediately threatens worker's income.
account_access_as_livelihood_gateway.source_ref: inferred from independent-contractor framing + deactivation risk

value.framing: platforms as algorithmic control mechanisms constraining worker autonomy
platforms as drivers of declining job quality and standard-employment erosion
platforms that adapt presentation by audience — worker, customer, regulator

four_framing_metaphors.quote: Platforms are seen as entrepreneurial incubators, digital cages, accelerants of precarity, and chameleons adapting to their environments

vallas_schor_alternative_framing.value: 'Permissive potentates' — platforms externalize responsibility (workers bear all risk) while still exercising concentrated power (algorithmic control, deactivation authority, opaque ratings)
vallas_schor_alternative_framing.quote: an alternative image of platforms: as permissive potentates that externalize responsibility and control over economic transactions while still exercising concentrated power

worker_solidarity_and_collective_action.value: Uber Boston drivers (Robinson 2017) built solidary ties to control supply and price of labor. 2019 one-day global strike to coincide with Uber IPO.

primary_interface.value: App-mediated — all task acquisition, routing, rating, and dispatch occurs via platform app. No human-dispatcher intermediary.

suitable_for_grounding_fields: daily_cashout_pattern (indirectly via earnings-volatility and supplement-vs-primary framing)
device_stability (implied: account = livelihood, so stability matters)
family_crisis_history (deactivation events, tip-stealing era, account compromise)
not_suitable_for_grounding_fields: corridor_country / language_mix (not a gig-worker demographic dimension in this paper)
persona_grounding_implications.behavioral_evidence_grade_when_used: C — academic behavioral research. Theoretical/review paper synthesizing empirical work by others; strongest for *structural* gig-worker context (algorithmic control, classification, precarity), weaker for individual-persona specifics.
persona_grounding_implications.caveat: Paper is from 2020 — predates major events like Prop 22 (2020 California ballot), multiple state-level classification rulings, and post-COVID gig-economy shifts. For persona-fraud-vector grounding, cross-reference with FinCEN FTA (account takeover, synthetic ID) and FTC Sentinel (BEC, imposter scams).
